title: All of the Guest Stars and Cameos on HBO Max’s ‘Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness’ (So Far)
full_text: Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All July 24, 2026 9:54pm Ike Barinholtz as Henry Ford and Larry David as a rabbi in Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness' Photograph by John Johnson/HBO Logo text Larry David has returned to HBO Max with the American history-centered sketch comedy show Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness , following the conclusion of his long-running series Curb Your Enthusiasm — and it’s not just executive producers Barack and Michelle Obama who are along for the ride. Dozens of celebrity guests have joined the comedian to fill out the cast of historical figures. This is not just a few cameos here and there — each episode of Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness has over a dozen celebrity guests, and the roster ranges from a few of David’s co-stars on Curb to the late Rob Reiner , in what became his final screen performance. Major Hollywood stars including Samuel L. Jackson and Lin-Manuel Miranda don the wigs and garb of decades and centuries past alongside television’s biggest names, like Jerry Seinfeld and Jon Hamm. The Hollywood Reporter is watching the series closely to make sure all these stars are accounted for — after all, they deserve some credit for spending time working with L.D. Related Stories News Crooked Media and a Former Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton Comms Exec Are Making a Political Show About the South (Exclusive) Movies From Michelle Obama's White House to Sundance Chair: The Extraordinary Second Act of Ebs Burnough New episodes of Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness air Friday nights at 9 p.m. on HBO and stream on HBO Max. Episode 1 – “Livingston” President Barack Obama as Himself; Samuel L. Jackson as The Narrator; Henry Winkler as John Hancock; Chris Parnell as Benjamin Franklin; Alan Tudyk as Thomas Jefferson; Alison Becker as Spectator 1; Mary Sohn as Spectator 2; Rodney J. Hobbs as Spectator 3; Richard Kind as Thomas Watson; Jake Reiner as Private Wallace; Mike Castle as Private Smith; Michael Chiklis as Sergeant; and Jurnee Smollett as Rosa Parks. The series opens with an appearance by one of its EPs and a familiar face to all: former President Barack Obama, whose Higher Ground Productions is behind the historical sketch comedy show. Obama praises the nation he led for eight years as it reaches its semiquincentennial and dunks on David a bit — because why not? He’s America’s most beloved curmudgeon. The intro gives way to narration from Samuel L. Jackson, a go-to voiceover these days, giving Morgan Freeman a run for his money. The first sketch has Winkler, Parnell and Tudyk as our founding fathers as they shut down the additions David’s Robert Livingston is trying to include in the grievances section of the Declaration of Independence. Next up, David portrays Alexander Graham Bell, forced to make awkward conversation with Curb cast member and national treasure Kind as Thomas Watson, as Bell debuts the telephone to a crowd of revelers already demanding text messaging and a variety of color options for the new invention. The annoying crowd features sitcom stalwarts Alison Becker ( Parks and Recreation ), Mary Sohn ( A.P. Bio ) and Rodney J. Hobbs ( The Office , Modern Family ). The third sketch involves WWI trench warfare, where David portrays a cowardly soldier under the command of a sergeant, played by none other than The Shield ‘s Michael Chiklis; his fellow soldiers are Comedy Bang Bang and Curb alum Mike Castle and Jake Reiner, the son of the late Rob Reiner (who also appeared on Curb ). The premiere episode closes with David as an irritating bus passenger who sits next to famed civil rights icon Rosa Parks, perfectly cast with Jurnee Smollett in the role. Episode 2 – “Farewell” Samuel L. Jackson as The Narrator; Rita Wilson as Mavis Lewis; Jerry Seinfeld as William Clark; Matthew Jones as Tilden’s Aide; Rich Fulcher as Tilden’s Aide; Larry Wilmore as Barney; Kaley Cuoco as Gloria, the Widow; Colton Dunn as Dominic the Soup Server; Rob Reiner as George Washington; Jimmy Kimmel as Crowd Member; and Allan Havey as Crowd Member. The second episode opens with a reunion between the two creators of the greatest sitcom of all time: Larry David and Jerry Seinfeld. The comedy duo behind the ’90s hit Seinfeld portrays explorers Lewis and Clark, whose landmark military mission, commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson, mapped the newly acquired Louisiana Territory and sought a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The gag is that the two are drinking buddies and it’s a bit too convenient they’re off to explore together for years on their own — as noted by Rita Wilson as Mavis Lewis, Meriwether Lewis’s long-suffering wife. David then skewers the Electoral College as he portrays Samuel Tilden, who won the popular vote in the 1876 presidential election but fell one vote shy of an Electoral College majority, ultimately losing to Rutherford B. Hayes. Ranting ensues as Matthew Jones, a Curb alum, and Rich Fulcher of The Mighty Boosh portray his aides. Next, in a Great Depression-set segment, David is joined by Larry Wilmore (formerly of late-night fame) and the incomparable Colton Dunn ( Superstore , Parks and Recreation ), and, in a series highlight, Kaley Cuoco as a grieving widow David is trying to use to cut in line for bread for his soup. Finally, the episode ends with the much-talked-about final screen appearance of Rob Reiner; here he portrays George Washington as he discusses term limits for the U.S. presidency in front of a gathered crowd. It’s all a setup for David’s townsman to take veiled swipes at President Trump, who is not named but we all know who L.D. is talking about. Jimmy Kimmel delightfully turns up in some meta-commentary on his forever feud with Trump, too. Episode 3 – “McCarthy” Samuel L. Jackson as The Narrator; Lou DiMaggio as Colonial Man; Lin-Manuel Miranda as Michael Finney; Jordan Black as Samuel Cooper; Brad Morris as Joseph Warren; J.B. Smoove as Jonesy Dean Sharpe; Armoire Tru Valentino as Ottoman Jon Hamm as Orville Wright; Sean Hayes as Wilbur Wright; Michael McKean as Joseph Welch; and Rob Huebel as Senator Mundt. The episode opens with David again playing his usual “guy caught up in a real historical moment” role as he crashes the Boston Tea Party [see flag No. 2 above]. Lin-Manuel Miranda, in fun stunt casting given his Broadway Revolutionary War pedigree from Hamilton , steals the scene as one of the Tea Party ringleaders. Comedian Lou DiMaggio appears too, playing off David’s character being left out of the rebellion. Speaking of scene stealers, J.B. Smoove’s character Jonesey makes a stop along the Underground Railroad, flabbergasting David’s host with his demands and, soon, his arriving friends. Next, David plays a fictional, less-than-heroic Wright sibling squabbling with his wife (Isla Fisher) over her critique of his butter-churning skills, while Jon Hamm and Sean Hayes play the actual Orville and Wilbur Wright preparing for the first flight. The episode’s closing and most talked-about segment features David himself playing Senator Joseph McCarthy. It also features SNL alum and Better Call Saul ‘s Michael McKean as attorney Joseph Welch, delivering the famous “Have you no decency, sir?” rebuttal, and Rob Huebel ( Human Giant , Transparent ) as a senator helping moderate one of the infamous hearings. Episode 4 – “Deepthroat” Samuel L. Jackson as The Narrator; Beck Bennett as Bob Woodward; Ike Barinholtz as Henry Ford; Diallo Riddle as John Appleton; Katie Aselton as Sylvia Jordana Brewster; Beatrice Merle Dandridge as Clementine; Andrea Savage as Cordelia; Rory Scovel as Jefferson Davis; Judy Gold as Evelyn; Adam Lustick as Jonas Salk; and Gregg “Jeep” Perrie as Bobby. The Watergate scandal gets the Larry David treatment: in the first sketch of the fourth episode, he portrays “Deep Throat,” the anonymous source who leaked details of the hotel break-in to Washington Post reporters. But David’s leaker doesn’t provide any useful information to SNL alum Beck Bennett’s Woodward when they meet in a parking lot — just trivial nonsense. Next up, Ike Barinholtz plays the notoriously antisemitic Henry Ford, less than thrilled to be showing his new vehicle to David’s rabbi character. David then portrays President James Buchanan, hitting on each passing lady at a party where he’s introduced the concept of passed appetizers in lieu of dinner. Jordana Brewster of the Fast & Furious movies and The Other Two , and The League ‘s Katie Aselton, are among the unfortunate ladies to cross his path; Diallo Riddle ( Marlon , South Side ) is Buchanan’s assistant, John Appleton. The big talker of the episode is saved for the finale, with David reviving an old stand-up bit as the overly proud mother of Jonas Salk, Dora, bragging on her son to her neighbor Evelyn about his discovery of the polio vaccine. It gets personal as David mocks his former friend and former co-star Cheryl Hines’ husband, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Soon a young man named Bobby turns up to naysay, telling Dora Salk, “That vaccine’s gonna kill people. It’s gonna give them heart attacks!” A parody of the stark politics of the MMR vaccine ensues, as only David could script. Episode 5 – “Lincoln” Samuel L. Jackson as The Narrator; Don Johnson as Doc Holiday; Timothy Olyphant as Wyatt Earp; Johnno Wilson as Virgil Earp; Marc Menchaca as Joseph Clanton; Maximo Salas as Young Clanton; Bill Hader as Abraham Lincoln; Kathryn Hahn as Mary Todd Lincoln; Lennon Parham as Laura Keene; Jay Renshaw as John Wilkes Booth; and Seth Morris as Andrew Johnson. Only two historical moments get the Larry David treatment in the fifth installment of the sketch series, but they are two pretty big moments. First, we’re at the O.K. Corral with Wyatt Earp (Timothy Olyphant) and Doc Holliday (Don Johnson), as a classic Curb -style obnoxious conversation about logistics gets applied to the location and timing of the famous shootout on Oct. 26, 1881. Marc Menchaca ( Curb ‘s Klansman Joe) plays a cowboy who calls out L.D.’s “pig-parking” job; Johnno Wilson as Virgil Earp and Maximo Salas as Young Clanton round out the cast of outlaws. Abraham Lincoln’s strained relationship with his wife, Mary Todd Lincoln, became Broadway fodder recently with Cole Escola’s Tony Award-winning turn in Oh, Mary! , and now it’s David’s turn to give us his take on the mentally unstable first lady. Bill Hader of SNL and Barry gives us a put-upon Lincoln who, in the sketch, connives with his chief of staff, Lawrence Butterfield, to get rid of Mary at Ford’s Theatre. A game of telephone ensues, with Lincoln wedged between the two as they watch Our American Cousin from box seats. The sketch’s second half has Butterfield and Mary arguing over a stolen sweater in another moment that could be straight out of Curb . This story was originally published on July 17, and has been updated as new episodes release. THR

title: Donald Trump Delivers Rally-Like Hour Of Rehash In White House Correspondents’ Dinner Speech
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Ted Johnson , Dade Hayes July 24, 2026 8:08pm President Donald Trump speaks during the re-scheduled White House Correspondents Dinner in Washington, DC. Eric Lee/Getty Images Speaking at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner on Friday, Donald Trump delivered an hour-long speech blending shopworn rally material with a string of leaden one-liners. He was making his first appearance as president at the dinner, which had to be rescheduled last Aprtil after a shooter attempted to rush the ballroom and was subdued by the Secret Service. While presidents for decades have long used the event’s keynote slot to zing reporters to varying degrees, Trump lapsed into rally mode, only deviating for some personal broadsides at members of the press, marbled with references to their appearance. Related Stories News Trump Celebrity Supporters: Famous Folks In Favor Of The 47th President Politics White House Responds After Alan Ritchson Urges Trump “Go To Jail” Over Epstein Files After one quip about an elderly U.S. senator’s sex life drew crickets, Trump asked, “Does anybody get that? I thought that was actually great. That was actually the only thing I thought was good in this whole frickin’ stupid speech. It was the only good one, and that went down with not exactly great laughter.” Watch on Deadline Over the rest of the meandering speech (watch the whole thing below), Trump seemed to recognize that many of his would-be jokes were not landing. There were few laughs or reactions at all beyond squirming or fidgeting as he veered in stream-of-consciousness fashion from topic to topic. “Tonight’s event is even crazier than the last time,” Trump said. “It’s so successful that I’ve been informed by CBS News’ David Ellison” (Ellison is CEO of CBS parent Paramount) that “next year, they’re going to call it the Trump White House Correspondents’ Dinner.” Changing the name, he added, “is the only way you’re going to get me back here.” The hour-long speech tested the patience of all but the fiercest Trump loyalists in attendance. The audience only sporadically showed a notable reaction, with long periods of near-silence prevailing. Once Trump’s remarks concluded and mentalist Oz Pearlman took the stage, a number of guests streamed toward the exits. Compared with April’s event at the Hilton, the ballroom at the Waldorf-Astoria is much smaller. Trump cabinet members mingled with reporters in an aisle near one of Paramount’s tables. Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim was at the dinner just a couple of hours after the decision to push back the company’s planned merger with Warner Bros. Discovery amid an antitrust challenge. At a Paramount table with Delrahim were cabinet members Pete Hegseth and presidential advisor Stephen Miller and his wife Katie Miller. Also at the event: Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert Kennedy Jr. and his wife Cheryl Himes, as well as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was at the center of one of Pearlman’s mental feats. Prior to Trump’s remarks, there were some awkward moments onstage as annual awards were given out, including to some journalists behind investigations of the president. As Wall Street Journal reporters accepted an honor for their Jeffrey Epstein story, Trump shook their hands and then threw his hands up in the air and smiled a bit. Wolf Blitzer, who was presenting the award, noted that he sued the WSJ over the story for $20 billion . Once at the lectern, Trump went after Josh Dawsey, one of the WSJ winners, and CNN host Kaitlan Collins with highly personal digs, but the room fell nearly silent as the would-be laugh lines were delivered. Weijia Jiang, outgoing president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, was stone-faced as Trump went into the would-be-roast-like digressions. CNN even released a statement during the speech, defending its journalists. The president appeared to have a set of prepared jokes, but he frequently veered off script, or their subjects seemed to remind him of an aside. The result was a speech that weaved through familiar political attacks, like on Adam Schiff’s appearance, to an extended riff on his plans for a White House ballroom. At one point, he pointed to details on the chandeliers at the Waldorf Astoria venue, which he built and previously operated as a Trump hotel. Some of his biting insults at the press were perhaps more muted than they otherwise would have been, given the sheer length of the speech and the topics covered. When Pearlman took the stage, he noted that Trump had made “an announcement that he will attending next year’s event. I thought he was going to speaking until next year, actually.” Trump had been scheduled to speak at the April dinner, but it was interrupted and then ended after a gunman breached a security barricade. The incident took place just outside the Washington Hilton ballroom, but shots could be heard among dinner guests. That sent the Secret Service scrambling to remove Trump and Vice President JD Vance from the dais, as well as other guests seated in the ballroom.

title: Guillermo Del Toro Assures “No Godd*mn AI” Used In ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ 3D Re-Release — Comic-Con
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn White House Responds After Alan Ritchson Urges Trump “Go To Jail” Over Epstein Files Kalshi Threatens Netflix With Defamation Suit Over “Misleading” Prediction Market Doc Trailer Weird Al Yankovic Says He Turned Down Seven-Figure Riyadh Comedy Fest Gig: “It Makes Me Feel Icky” View All July 24, 2026 7:40pm Doug Jones and Ivana Baquero in 'Pan's Labyrinth' (2006) Picturehouse/Courtesy Everett Collection As Guillermo Del Toro brings Pan’s Labyrinth back to theaters 20 years later, he’s sticking to tried-and-true restoration techniques. During Friday’s Hall H panel for the movie’s milestone anniversary at San Diego Comic-Con, the 3x Oscar winner reinforced his stance on using “absolutely no goddamn AI ” in the 3D re-release, which premieres Oct. 9 in theaters. “I said, ‘Absolutely no goddamn AI,'” said Del Toro to applause. “It’s much more expensive. I don’t care. The thing is, what we’re protecting is the beauty and the redeeming power of art.” Related Stories News ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’: Cineverse 20th Anniversary Re-Release Sets Fall Date; Fathom Boards As Distrib Partner News Guillermo Del Toro Would “Rather Die” Than Use Generative AI: “I Am Not Interested” Del Toro’s latest comments come after he has frequently denounced generative AI, saying last year that he’d “ rather die ” than use it in his filmmaking. “Fuck AI!” he has declared on more than one occasion. Watch on Deadline At Friday’s panel, the Mexican auteur also recalled the crew of Pan’s Labyrinth not initially understanding his wild vision of a dark fantasy set during the Spanish Civil War of 1936-’39. Doug Jones in ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ (2006) (Picturehouse/Courtesy Everett Collection) “We had a lot of adversity in the movie,” said Del Toro. “And a lot of the crew was very skeptical. They would see a faun come in in the middle of a civil war movie, and they would say, ‘This fucker is crazy.’ But I remember the first time I knew, we were shooting the Pale Man.” Re-enacting the Pale Man’s now iconic moment of holding up his own eyes in his hands to see, Del Toro noted that was the moment the crew was on board with his vision. “I said, ‘Ah, see?'” he recalled. title: Trump Says White House Correspondents Dinner Is ‘Largest Group of Trump Derangement Syndrome People Ever Put Together at One Time’
full_text: Breaking News Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial Jul 24, 2026 7:37pm PT Trump Says White House Correspondents Dinner Is ‘Largest Group of Trump Derangement Syndrome People Ever Put Together at One Time’ President jokes that David Ellison will change event's name to the 'Trump White House Correspondents Dinner' next year By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Trump Says White House Correspondents Dinner Is ‘Largest Group of Trump Derangement Syndrome People Ever Put Together at One Time’ 8 hours ago Paramount Faces Drawn-Out Battle With State AGs: ‘They Saw the Writing on the Wall’ 10 hours ago Warner Bros. Discovery Sues Amazon, Accusing It of ‘Lawless Employee Shopping Spree’ Including Poaching HBO Veteran Pia Barlow 15 hours ago See All Eric Lee/Getty Images President Donald Trump attended his first-ever White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner, with this year’s rescheduled gala held Friday evening in Washington, D.C., and delivered some pointed remarks to the assembled journalists in a rambling speech that stretched on for just over an hour — and during which he insulted several journalists, politicians and celebs that he’s sparred with. “I am delighted to be here at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. Amazing people, a lot of people that I like,” Trump said. “Some I don’t like at all, but I respect most of them.” Related Stories Confused by ‘The Odyssey’? All the Timelines, Monsters and Greek Myths Explained Whoopi Goldberg Slams Transphobic Critics of Elliot Page’s Casting in ‘The Odyssey’: ‘Then Don’t Go See It… Why Do You Care Who’s Cast in It?’ At first, Trump seemed unsure of the tone he wanted to impart, and suggested that — compared with barbs he was planning to deliver at the original WHCA dinner, which was disrupted by a gun-wielding attacker — he was pulling his punches. “I said, ‘What do we do here? Is this supposed to be fun? Am I supposed to be serious? Am I supposed to be a comedian?’ So I guess you said, maybe a little bit of everything.” Popular on Variety But Trump quickly started bashing the press. “This evening it’s really all about the fake news media and your handling of prizes — writing and producing and performing made-up stories like the Academy Awards,” Trump said. The Academy Awards “used to be the the epitome of ratings outside of the Super Bowl… Now it’s down in the dumps. Nobody wants to watch it anymore because they took on Trump. They hit me all night long.” He told the journalists, “when I’m gone. You’re all going to be broke. Your business model is going to be finished. No, it’s true. When I’m not around, you’re going to be broke. There’s not going to be anybody to report on. Nobody gives a damn about anybody else.” Trump said that “mostly, I’ve given up on you and the media, so that now I just gave up on you, and I’m number one on TikTok. Did you see that?… I gave up on you, people. I gave up on traditional press, and it obviously worked because we did win in a landline” (he meant “landslide,” but that is not true). Trump boasted that “I was able to get [TikTok] sold to a group of very wealthy people, mostly Americans.” Trump said he did not attend past WHCA dinners because “I thought the press treated me very, very unfairly, and I don’t know. I think I made the right decision because they need to go where maybe you’re not wanted, but they did want me. They wanted me for ratings, and they wanted me for other reasons, but not for love. And I said, ‘You know, I’m not going to go.’ First time that ever happened… And I didn’t go for four years because I got treated terribly by the press.” This year, Trump noted, the WHCA decided not to have a comedian. “They considered using Jimmy Kimmel, Jimmy Fallon,” Trump said. “These guys — they’re terrible. They’re terrible. Stephen Colbert. These are people without talent… They have no talent, but they are not comedians. They’re not funny people. They’re angry people. They’re sick people.” Trump took the podium at 9:33 p.m. and held forth for about 64 minutes. Trump joked that Paramount CEO David Ellison, whose company owns CBS News (“He bought it, spent a lot of money, and he’s going to make, I think, fantastic changes and keep some of the great stuff going”), told him that next year Ellison will rename the WHCA dinner “the Trump White House Correspondents’ Dinner.” “He told me that, and I like that very much. We’re going to change the name of it, OK?” Trump said, alluding to his unsuccessful effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center . He also said at another point in his talk, “I, for one, wish Bari Weiss all the best at CBS News. She’s a wonderful woman,” which drew an audible murmur from the audience. He said White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt “may have one of the hardest jobs in the White House” because she has to “deal with all of you all the time, and you can be very difficult. You can be very, very difficult people. But I’m probably being a little bit oversensitive. Sometimes I really do think that some of you don’t like me.” He quipped, “This place is the really the largest group of Trump derangement syndrome people ever put together at one time, I suspect,” eliciting a smattering of laughter. (The president apparently believes that Trump derangement syndrome is a real medical condition .) Trump slammed some of his favorite perceived enemies. He said the winner of the lowest ratings and the “lowest IQ on television” was “actually Don Lemon,” whom Trump called “the dumbest man on television. I said, you know, when you say some things, you never make a comeback. It’s not like, ‘Oh gee, hey Don, let’s have dinner some night.'” Trump also took aim at CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins, who won the 2026 WHCA award for broadcast for her coverage of Trump’s confrontation in the Oval Office showdown with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky in February 2025. Trump said, “I want to personally congratulate CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on receiving her award” but said it “was all about me. It’s a fake. She shouldn’t get the award. It was a fake, but I didn’t mind.” (In a statement issued as Trump was still speaking, Mark Thompson, chairman and CEO of CNN Worldwide, said: “We stand by our journalists and the integrity and fair mindedness with which the CNN team reports the news. Honest, accurate journalism may sometimes irritate politicians, but our right to report and present that reporting to the public without government interference is fully protected by the U.S. Constitution. CNN will continue to exercise this right.”) Trump then went on a weird tangent about Collins, calling her “a young, active woman” but that “she never smiles. I said, ‘Kaitlan, do you ever smile? Smile. You have a nice position. You’re at CNN fake news. You should be a happy person. Just smile, Kaitlan. Just smile.'” Then Trump tried to joke that Collins had signed “a major new sponsorship. But then I informed her that it wasn’t her on the Bud Light can. It was Dylan Mulvaney,” Trump said, referring to transgender influencer who was enlisted by the beer company in 2023, a campaign that suffered a huge backlash. “Dylan Mulvaney cost Bud like $35 million in market cap. It was the worst commercial ever made, by the way. For those few people that want to hear that, most people don’t care, but I would. I wouldn’t want to hire Dylan anytime soon,” said Trump. About another CNN anchor, Anderson Cooper, Trump said: “I like Anderson actually because he’s covered me well for many years, and he went bad as soon as I went for politics. But for years, he loved interviews. I did so many interviews with him, and he was great. But you know, he’s got a little different persuasion than me, in many ways actually.” Trump also lashed out at California Gov. Gavin Newsom, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer, Rosie O’Donnell (a “sick older woman”), CNN’s Jake Tapper and Bruce Springsteen. About Springsteen, Trump said: “What the hell happened to that guy? He looks like hell… I’m sure he doesn’t like the way I look, but I don’t look so bad.” He complained that Springsteen made “four political speeches in his three-hour show,” leading Trump to joke, “The tour has been renamed ‘Bored in the USA,’ and his new song was so bad.” Trump, of course, has had a hostile relationship with the press. He not only routinely complains that news outlets are “fake news” and insults individual journalists but he has also sued multiple news outlets over coverage he dislikes, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and CBS News’ “60 Minutes.” At the WHCA dinner, the Wall Street Journal reporters behind the paper’s story about a birthday letter purportedly written by Trump to Jeffrey Epstein won the $10,000 Katharine Graham Award for Courage and Accountability award. Trump, who has denied he penned the Epstein letter, filed a lawsuit over the story, demanding $20 billion in damages. The Journal’s lawyers called Trump’s lawsuit “an affront to the First Amendment.” A judge dismissed his original suit but Trump refiled the complaint in May 2026 and the case is pending. At the dinner, Trump awkwardly shook the hands of the Journal reporters who were there to receive the prize, then threw up his hands in mock resignation and returned to his seat. “This has not been an easy evening. All these awards… Do I get a say in those awards?” Trump joked during his remarks. Near the end of his long speech, Trump joked that he would run for a fourth term — and he donned a “Trump 2028” hat — repeating his baseless claim that he actually won the 2020 U.S. presidential election. (He did not.) Trump said he plans to return to the correspondents’ dinner in 2027. Meanwhile, Trump also made a joke at the expense of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of Health and Human Services. “Bobby Kennedy’s right here. He personally ran over the cow in his car… He brought it here for you to eat tonight,” Trump said. “So it’s very fresh. And Bobby also suggested an appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill. But we drew the line at that, Cheryl. We said, no, we’re not going to do that. We’re not doing that. We love Bobby.” Friday’s WHCA dinner took place at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in D.C. It featured a performance by mentalist Oz Pearlman, whereas the association has traditionally invited a comedian to roast the sitting president. The WHCA dinner was rescheduled after the first gathering, on April 25, was interrupted by an evident assassination attempt on Trump . The gunman who crashed through security at the Washington Hilton was apprehended and charged. Trump spent time discussing the April attack in his remarks, thanking the law enforcement personnel who subdued the suspect. Outgoing WHCA president Weijia Jiang, senior White House correspondent for CBS News, delivered opening remarks at the start of the event. title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ Creator on Writing Season 2 After Buzzy Launch: “I Learned a Lot About What You Don’t Need”
full_text: Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All July 24, 2026 7:30pm Matthew Rhys on 'Widow's Bay.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Logo text The writing process has just begun for the second season of Apple TV ‘s latest hit series Widow’s Bay . Show creator Katie Dippold participated in Collider’ s Showrunners on Showrunning panel at San Diego Comic-Con on Friday, where she opened up about the project’s startling success . Starring Matthew Rhys as the mayor of a New England island that the residents are convinced is haunted, Widow’s Bay quickly became one of television’s buzziest shows after its April launch and went on to land a whopping 19 Emmy Award nominations , including best comedy series. Related Stories Movies Rick Moranis Makes Comic-Con Debut for 'Spaceballs' Sequel TV 'Lanterns' Trailer Reveals Sinestro and Its Manhunter Threat as Aaron Pierre Wins Over Comic-Con “It took a long time,” Dippold said about how soon she got a sense that the show had picked up as many fans as it did. She joked that she remains “terrified” of Reddit but eventually took enough of a look on the social media platform to see that the amount of discussion about Widow’s Bay was increasing wildly. “Seeing that was really shocking.” The writer, also known for her work on such features as The Heat and Snatched , explained that she did not know that the series had been renewed for a second season until just before the news went public. “But I was still always hoping and thinking about it,” she continued, pointing out that the writers room for season two started earlier this week. “It’s a great room, and then we’re going to be writing for the next 20 weeks.” Dippold noted that her goal is to begin filming next year for the show that also stars Kate O’Flynn, Kevin Carroll, Dale Dickey, Kingston Rumi Southwick and Stephen Root. As for lessons from the initial season that the first-time showrunner plans to incorporate for the second one, Dippold said, “I learned pretty quickly in making it.” Dippold pointed out that she felt that the comedy worked because the actors played things straight and dramatic: “Throughout the process, it was making sure everything served that, and so that’s top of mind going into season two. Also, the scripts were longer and pretty dense. I had to make last-minute cuts for time, so I’ll just be more mindful of that because we didn’t need that much.” She added, “In the edit, I just could see, ‘Oh, you actually didn’t need any of this stuff anyway.’ I learned a lot about what you don’t need and getting to things quicker.” In her review of Widow’s Bay for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Angie Han wrote, “At its best, Widow’s Bay highlights the blurry line between comedy and horror.” THR

title: President Trump Roasts Media at Rescheduled, Pared-Down White House Correspondents’ Dinner
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All July 24, 2026 7:25pm U.S. President Donald Trump and CBS News senior White House correspondent and WHCA President Weijia Jiang salute during the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, DC, on July 24, 2026. Photo by Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images President Trump appeared at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner, which took place in Washington, D.C. on Friday with a new location and a drastically reduced list of attendees, following the cancellation of the event in April after a gunman fired shots as the event was underway. Moved to the Waldorf Astoria in the nation’s capital instead of the Washington Hilton and reduced from 2,600 guests down to around 680, it was less a star-studded event that each year sees celebrity guests brush elbows with reporters and editors as they sit with the politicians they cover — the optics of which are criticized each year by journalists and critics alike. Related Stories General News Donald Trump Booed at World Cup Final General News Donald Trump Drops Part of His $10 Billion Defamation Lawsuit Against the BBC For the make-up dinner, the WHCA is also bringing back the Secret Service member who survived the April shooting, when 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen , who allegedly intended to target multiple Trump administration officials, was arrested near the screening area outside the banquet hall after running past the security checkpoint. Plus, the dinner honored the Washington Hilton staff who stayed on the scene and continued tending to rattled guests. Elements of the first dinner remained. The awards were handed out; mentalist Oz Pearlman, who got just one private trick for the White House press secretary at the first dinner before gunshots caused chaos, returned to deliver some levity; and ahead of the event, a group of hundreds of former journalists and press freedom groups sent a letter to the WHCA. Now, they were urging the association to capitalize on Trump’s attendance by calling him out for his administration’s attacks on First Amendment rights, which include recently subpoenaing New York Times reporters over their coverage and threatening to revoke licenses of broadcasters. The president took to the stage around 9:30 p.m. ET and brought up the attempted attack early in his much-anticipated speech, which has been speculated upon heavily in April and again ahead of the July event. Traditionally, the dinner’s speeches are a roast of the attendees and the president himself. “The attempted mass murder at the Washington Hilton-that’s what it could have been-was an assault on our democracy itself,” Trump said. “A very serious situation. Many of you were there with me, and some showed extreme bravery, like Pete Hegseth, Steve Miller, Tom Holman. Really, they were standing on tables. And most of you were under the table,” he said to Friday night’s attendees, which got some laughs. Following some begrudging admiration of the press and the constitutional freedom of speech, the notion of a third Trump term, the White House ballroom project, and Robert Kennedy Jr. mowing down the cow served at dinner with his car were some of Trump’s early jokes. They garnered a new laugh, but his first zinger to fall completely flat came soon and involved a rapper and MAGA convert whom he recently had at a White House event. “After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, ‘Get down! Get down!’ which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking,” he said, referring to the dance. “Do you believe it? Get down. She’s the only one that really understood what that meant.” Trump’s speech began to meander as he at first reminisced about the Waldorf Astoria in the 1980s and moved to a number of topics and name-dropped celebrities not in the room and with whom he has personal gripes, some going back for decades. Rosie O’Donnell, Bette Midler and Bruce Springsteen all got a mention, with the latter’s looks as he ages compared to the president’s own. Trump joked that his live show, where he was railing about the administration’s policies, was now called “Bored in the U.S.A.” Attendees were caught on camera in footage streamed live by the Associated Press looking bored and irritated as Trump’s speech went past the 20-minute mark, and it was clear this was not going to be the biting speech some anticipated Trump’s typical airing, but another airing of grievance from Trump peppered with a few jokes that landed with a thud. Even the president was critical of some of the jokes when they received no laughs. At one point, he referred to the “governor of Chicago,” presumably billionaire Gov. of Illinois, J.B. Pritzker, while discussing a staged fight among politicians. “I would say I could mention the governor of Chicago, but I’m going to mention instead Jerry Nadler, and they’re fighting for a big piece of cheesecake, big fat piece of cheesecake,” he said to zero audible laughs. “Who the hell wrote that line?” During the airing of grievances portion of his speech on a night celebrating journalists, Trump, as expected, tore into reporters for perceived unfair treatment, and specifically mentioned CNN anchors Kaitlan Collins (an award recipient honored earlier in the night) and Jake Tapper (a multiple winner of the multiple recipient of the White House Correspondents’ Association Merriman Smith Award). Following mentions of late-night hosts Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert, whom he called talentless, Trump also admitted that he truly hates some people. “They thought about going with a professional clown for entertainment, but Adam ‘Shifty’ Schiff was not available,” Trump joked. “You know he’s known — I hate some people. You know, I shouldn’t say the surprise. I’m not supposed to hate him. I’m supposed to love everybody, but he’s a terrible person. He’s a liar, and I called him watermelon head because he has the largest head I’ve ever seen with the smallest neck, pencil neck. How does that big fat ugly head stand on a on a little pencil, pencil, pencil neck?” After about an hour of a speech that turned nasty fast and featured few funny lines, Trump ended the speech on an up note and even praised the journalists in the room and their profession. “We have the hottest country anywhere in the world, and we’re going to keep it going,” he said. “And I just want to say, this is a room I have tremendous respect for the people in this room. Sometimes I don’t feel you treat me fair. Maybe you do. I don’t know. I don’t feel that. But sometimes you treat me very fairly, and I have a lot of respect for your profession. Your profession is amazing. And I just want to thank you for having me. And it’s been fun.” THR

title: Rick Moranis Makes Comic-Con Debut for ‘Spaceballs’ Sequel
full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit Plus Icon Borys Kit Senior Film Writer View All July 24, 2026 6:48pm 'Spaceballs: The New One' panel at Comic-Con 2026. Chris Frawley / Amazon MGM Studios Logo text Laughs and an appreciation of Rick Moranis were plentiful as Amazon MGM’s Spaceballs : The New One , a sequel to the 1987 Mel Brooks Star Wars parody, flew into San Diego Comic-Con ’s cavernous Hall H Friday afternoon. One of the panel’s biggest attractions was seeing Moranis, the comedian who appeared in seminal 1980s films such as Ghostbusters and Honey, I Shrunk the Kid , make his first ever appearance. The actor played villain Dark Helmet in the original 1987 movie but has been largely absent from movies and television for most of this century, so his return with the Spaceballs sequel is headline making. Related Stories TV 'Lanterns' Trailer Reveals Sinestro and Its Manhunter Threat as Aaron Pierre Wins Over Comic-Con TV 'Rick and Morty' Spinoff 'President Curtis' Scores Early Season 2 Renewal at Adult Swim After a “comb the audience” joke, a callback to a line in the original movie that revealed the comedian to be in the audience wearing an oversized Darth Vader-style helmer, Moranis hopped up the stage to a standing ovation and chants of “Rick! Rick! Rick!” “You made our childhoods better,” said Kevin Smith, who ably moderated the panel. Moranis sat between Josh Gad , one of the creative forces behind the sequel, and Daphne Zuniga, who played Princess Vespa in the original and returns for the sequel. Also on stage were director Josh Greenbaum, actors Keke Palmer and Lewis Pullman, and writers Dan Hernandez and Benji Samit. Gad described the origins of the sequel, recounting how he had been working on a Honey I Shrunk the Kids sequel with Moranis that ultimately fell apart, but did end up watching Moranis movies with his daughter. “We finished it and she goes, ‘Can we watch part 2?’” he said. “And I said, ‘There is no part 2.’ And she said, ‘Yeah, the weird little alien guy said there was going to be a part 2.’” When he replied, “Oh sweetie, that is called a joke,” she countered, “Well, why isn’t there a part 2?” That night, Gad said, he had a dream about the sequel and soon after was pitching Brooks and his producing partner. He threw in ideas refencing new Star Wars movies and characters such as The Force Awakens and Kylo Ren. Imitating Brooks, Gad summed up his reaction: “Josh, it sounds like you’ve really got your finger on the pulse. I don’t know half of what you’re talking about, but I really like it.” The comedic presence of Brooks, who appeared only by a recorded video early on in the panel where he thanked the nerds for keeping his movie alive close to 40 years, loomed large over Hall H. Amazon MGM bucked the Comic-Con trend by not having a trailer debut or showing any clips from the movie, but it did show videos of Brooks reuniting with Moranis, reuniting with original star Bill Pullman and Zuniga, and recording lines in a booth while praising — or not — the script. Greenbaum recounted meeting the comedy legend early on in the movie’s development, and when it was approaching time to being principal photography, he asked if the man had any words of advice. Brooks paused, and said yes. Greenbaum was thrilled. He leaned in. “Don’t say ‘Cut!’ first. It’s ‘Action!,’ and then ‘Cut!’” Brooks told him. The young director’s takeaway? “It was, don’t take this too seriously and go out there and have fun,” Greenbaum summed up. The new movie, Gad said, takes a look at the state of movies and nostalgia. “The industry it was parodying is a very different industry than this one 40 years later,” said Gad. “We all sort of talked thematically about this word ‘nostalgia.’ And we love movies that look back. We love sequels. We love continuing these stories we grew up with. We analyzed why that is and we thought Spaceballs was the perfect vehicle to catch us up with everything that’s happened in filmdom and in fan filmdom. Interjected Smith, “When they made the first one, there was a trilogy to make fun of. Now there’s a never-ending fount.” “We really wanted to dive into that,” Gad replied. The panel also featured a funny bit where Lewis Pullman read out a letter purportedly written by his father, Bill Pullman, about how great it was to be part of a family, while ignoring his own father-son relationship. And it also showed, on multiple screens, the purported plans of a Spaceballs cinematic universe, sketched out in decade-spanning movie “phases,” a shot at how Marvel Studios has unveiled timeline of its various movie plans. THR

title: Nick Hakim’s ‘I Can See’ Is a Hazy Alt-R&B Masterpiece: Album Review
full_text: Breaking News Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial Jul 24, 2026 6:28pm PT Nick Hakim’s ‘I Can See’ Is a Hazy Alt-R&B Masterpiece: Album Review By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Nick Hakim’s ‘I Can See’ Is a Hazy Alt-R&B Masterpiece: Album Review 9 hours ago Charli xcx Cranks Up the Guitars and Launches Her Post-‘Brat’ Era With the Razor-Sharp ‘Music, Fashion, Film’: Album Review 1 day ago Sienna Spiro Plays Intimate Benefit Concert for North Shore Animal League 2 days ago See All “Stoner R&B” is not an insult: It’s the opposite, a loose term to describe a sprawling genre of music that includes everything from Dijon and Frank Ocean to Brent Faiyaz and Jhene Aiko. It’s R&B that has smoked a strong blunt, with languid grooves, heavy bass, psychedelicized production and an unhurried vocal approach. Unlike the tight rhythms, choppy guitars and urgency of traditional R&B, it’s not in a hurry to get anywhere. When Nick Hakim first emerged in 2014 with his “Where Will We Go” EPs and subsequent albums, he was a bright new voice in the genre, but as the years went by, his music sailed further and further out until, by 2022’s “Cometa,” conventional song structures had pretty much drifted off. Related Stories Whoopi Goldberg Slams Transphobic Critics of Elliot Page’s Casting in ‘The Odyssey’: ‘Then Don’t Go See It… Why Do You Care Who’s Cast in It?’ Christopher Nolan Says 'The Odyssey's' Modern English Dialogue 'Was a No-Brainer' Even If 'It Might Bite Me on the Ass' and 'I Was Maybe Being Naïve' But his fourth and latest album, “I Can See,” is his most focused work to date — and despite the unhurried tempos and smoky vibes, it’s a very seriously structured set of songs, with multiple layers of his soft, soulful vocals and shimmering keyboards. “Real Here Now” is one of the most gorgeous R&B songs you’ll hear all year and is almost like an Usher song from a parallel universe, but as always his music has a crossover appeal that defies pigeonholing: The following song, “U Can Make It,” is a densely layered track built around a thudding electronic bass drum, echo-drenched piano and layers and layers of vocals. Popular on Variety The unusually hazy sound of this album is as vital as the songs — the vocals and instruments waft in and out of the mix like music from a passing car or sounds from the apartment next door; you’re not always sure exactly what you’re hearing, not that it matters. Equal parts electronic and organic, it pairs conventional snare and rimshot sounds with heavy digital bass, piano so heavily treated that it sounds like a warped calliope, and backing vocals that float in and out like a chorus of ghosts. After the more-conventionally structured songs of the album’s first half, the last few continue “Cometa”’s journey toward the cosmos, growing murkier and piling on effects reminiscent of dub reggae. Indeed, “I Can See” is a realm beyond alternative R&B — it’s more like R&B from a different planet. title: Paramount Faces Drawn-Out Battle With State AGs: ‘They Saw the Writing on the Wall’
full_text: Breaking News Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial Jul 24, 2026 5:54pm PT Paramount Faces Drawn-Out Battle With State AGs: ‘They Saw the Writing on the Wall’ By Gene Maddaus , Todd Spangler Getty Only a few days ago, the states’ antitrust challenge to the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger still looked like a speed bump. Now, it looks more like siege warfare — as Paramount has agreed to put the $111 million deal on hold for at least several months. In doing so, Paramount’s lawyers have effectively conceded that they were not likely to prevail in an upcoming fight over an injunction and will instead try to beat the states at trial. Related Stories Hollywood's Favorite Ugg Slippers (To Never Wear on a Christopher Nolan Set) How Long Can 'The Odyssey' Stay on Imax 70mm Screens? Nolan Fans Scramble as New Showtimes Sell Out 7 Weeks in Advance “I think they saw the writing on the wall,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Variety on Friday. “They saw that the outcome of a motion for a preliminary injunction was a fait accompli. The die was cast. They were going to lose. Otherwise, why not challenge it?” Popular on Variety David Ellison, Paramount Skydance ‘s chairman and CEO, had hoped to win a ruling denying the injunction by mid-September — allowing him to close the deal in time to avoid paying Warner Bros. shareholders millions of dollars a day. His lawyers pushed for a three-day evidentiary hearing in late August, where they could confront the states’ expert economist and undermine the states’ argument that the deal will result in illegal market concentration. But in a ruling on Thursday, Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin denied Paramount’s bid to speed up briefing on that request, signaling she was not inclined to go along with the multiday hearing. The judge had already granted a 28-day restraining order, finding that the states had made a “strong showing” that the merger was likely to harm competition, and the standard to get an injunction would be similar. Paramount could have opted to wait for the ruling and then immediately appeal to the 9th Circuit. But Nexstar tried to do that after its merger with Tegna was enjoined in April — and is still stuck in limbo with no assurance of resolution anytime soon. Paramount would have faced a similar delay, likely pushing any appellate relief into early 2027. So where does it go from here? To trial, where Paramount still believes it has the upper hand against what it terms “one of the weakest merger challenges in modern antitrust history.” The company hopes to get there as soon as possible, ideally before the end of 2026. Whenever a trial is held, it won’t come fast enough to avoid having to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders $7 million per day, starting on Sept. 30. But that is a cost that Paramount will have to bear to get the deal done. The 12-state coalition will push for a later date, arguing that it needs additional time to prepare. “We do think 2027 is appropriate,” Bonta said. “If the judge said April 2027, we would not disagree with that.” Paramount has agreed not to close the transaction until five days after the trial ruling or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first. Bonta argued that Paramount is pushing for a speedy resolution due to “business factors” and not due process considerations. “I’m sure they want a fast trial,” he said. “That’s based on other reasons, not what’s appropriate for a case of this magnitude.” The states will want extra time to obtain extensive discovery, including documents and depositions they were unable to get during their investigation. “Paramount and Warner Bros. were dragging their feet. They didn’t give us everything we wanted,” Bonta said. “If they wanted to have a trial quicker, they could have given us the information we asked for in the pre-litigation discovery process.” The trial will be held in Martinez-Olguin’s courtroom in Oakland, Calif., and could last two to three weeks or more. In the meantime, Paramount could seek to reopen settlement talks with the states. So far, Bonta said, the company has not offered the sort of structural remedies — that is, divestitures of cable or film distribution assets — that would have to be part of a deal. Bonta has said repeatedly that he is not interested in “behavioral” remedies, such as a consent decree guaranteeing a minimum number of film releases or 45-day theatrical windows, saying that those have proven ineffective in the past. “We’ve never gotten anything that would come close to addressing the concerns we’ve raised,” Bonta said. “We’re focused on litigation. We’ve built momentum and we look forward to taking that momentum into trial.” In its statement, Paramount argued that the strategic retreat was the best way to get to a decision on the merits of the deal as soon as possible. “This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers, and good for creators, a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached,” the company said. Bonta argued the opposite — and now it’s clear those arguments present more than a minor obstacle. “This merger, if it is able to go through, will hurt Americans, will hurt Californians,” he said. “It will raise their prices. title: Hollywood Royalty, Michelin-Starred Meal, Cartier Gift Bags: Inside Monaco’s Most Exclusive Event of the Year
full_text: × Skip to main content By Erin Lassner Plus Icon Erin Lassner E-Commerce Writer View All July 24, 2026 5:45pm Courtesy of The Red Cross If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission. The Monaco Grand Prix , the Rose Ball and the Red Cross Gala: the Monégasque social calendar’s trifecta of prestige. Serving as the pinnacle of black tie elegance, Monaco ‘s Red Cross Gala — or the Gala de la Croix-Rouge Monégasque, in French — is the yearly flagship fundraiser for the Monaco Red Cross, which, from 1958 to 1982, was presided over by none other than Grace Kelly , Princess of Monaco. Cut to the evening of July 18, 2026: Even without the Oscar-winning movie star’s physical presence, the Old Hollywood glamour at the 77th annual charity ball was palpable. Courtesy of AFP via Getty Images Prince Albert II and Princess Charlene of Monaco arrive at Sporting Monte-Carlo for the annual Red Cross Gala on July 18, 2026. Courtesy of The Red Cross On Saturday night at the Sporting Monte-Carlo, esteemed guests eagerly awaited the arrival of Prince Albert II and Princess Charlene, son and daughter-in-law of Grace Kelly and respective President and Vice-President of the Red Cross Society’s Monaco branch. Charlene, Princess of Monaco, statuesque as ever, channeled the timeless style of her late mother-in-law in a custom-made Elie Saab golden draped gown. The couple was joined by niece Camille Gottlieb, one of Kelly’s 11 grandchildren, plus the evening’s hosting duo, actress and model Estelle Lefébure and actor and comedian Michel Boujenah. Following arrivals, guests glided through a sea of white tablecloths to dine on a multi-course meal imagined by three-Michelin-starred chef Marcel Ravin. And while only one lucky winner walked away with the gala’s grand prize, a Cartier Grain de Café jewelry set fit with 58 total diamonds, every guest in attendance went home with a generous parting gift from the luxury House, a supple leather cardholder stamped with the Double C emblem. The gala’s grand prize, a Cartier Grain de Café jewelry set, gifted by the luxury House. Courtesy of The Red Cross On the heels of an otherworldly fireworks show and ahead of the jazz-inspired after party, guests enjoyed the world premiere of SOUL! Where Legends Come Back . This dance-inducing live show, which traces the journey of African-American music, is the newest original production by Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer (SBM), the luxury hospitality and entertainment company that doubles as the annual gala’s organizer and venue host. In many ways, SBM feels like — and, quite honestly, is — the brain behind much of Monaco’s social, cultural and hotel scene, with the sovereign city-state sitting at under one square mile. SBM’s crown jewel has to be the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo , a palatial escape located at Place du Casino in Monte Carlo, smack dab in the heart of Monaco. Widely regarded as one of the world’s most luxurious properties, Hôtel de Paris is every bit as breathtakingly lavish as you’d hope and expect. It, therefore, only makes sense that a conveyor belt of black cars promptly escorted guests from their accommodations and pre-event drinks to the main festivities at the Sporting Monte-Carlo. So what’s next on the Principality of Monaco’s social calendar? Well, you’ll have to consult Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer’s extensive annual agenda . title: Ralph W. Hemecker, Veteran TV Director of ‘Blue Bloods,’ ‘Once Upon a Time’ and More, Dies at 65
full_text: Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All July 24, 2026 5:08pm Ralph W. Hemecker Courtesy Hemecker Family Veteran TV director, writer, producer and showrunner Ralph W. Hemecker has died. He was 65. Hemecker, whose work spanned three decades and included directing 31 episodes of Blue Bloods and 28 episodes of Once Upon a Time , died July 10 at his home in Glendale. He also directed episodes of The X-Files, Millennium, Ghost Whisperer, Numb3rs, The Vampire Diaries, Nikita, V, Legends of Tomorrow, Quantico, Body of Proof, The Flash and Pacific Blue as well as the 2000 TNT TV movie Witchblade , going on to serve as showrunner, writer and executive producer of the Witchblade TV series across its two-season run from 2001 to 2002. Related Stories Movies Chuck Russell, Director of 'A Nightmare on Elm Street 3' and 'The Mask,' Dies at 74 Movies Chris Affleck, Mother of Oscar Winners Ben and Casey Affleck, Dies at 83 And he directed the pilot for Roar , starring a then little-known Heath Ledger, as well as the pilots for Lawless and Dead at 21 . Born on June 12, 1961, Ralph William Hemecker graduated from Bucknell University where he studied English, made short films and developed a passion for visual storytelling. He went on to take filmmaking courses at New York University and began his career in production and post-production. Some of his earliest directing work was on America’s Most Wanted , helming dramatic reenactments of real-life crimes, and he directed episodes of Silk Stalkings , on which he worked behind the scenes, as well as Renegade . “Some losses are impossible to put into words,” Once Upon a Time actress Lana Parrilla wrote in part on Instagram . “Ralph Hemecker was one of the kindest, most generous souls I’ve ever known. One of Once Upon a Time ’s defining directors. A truly passionate, beautiful man and my dear friend. I was lucky enough to shadow Ralph as a director as he knew Once , behind the camera, best. He was always carrying a camera in hand, staying up all night in the director’s office putting his shots together, studying the scripts and endlessly visiting sets in preparation. His passion was infectious. We always knew if Ralph was directing, we were in good hands.” Hemecker is survived by his two stepdaughters as well as his father, sister and brother; two nephews; one niece and one great-nephew. Hemecker admired the Navy SEALs’ courage, discipline, resilience and commitment to service, and he was inspired by their leadership principles. As a result, in lieu of flowers, his family asks that memorial donations be made to the SEAL Future Foundation in Hemecker’s memory. A celebration of Hemecker’s life will be announced at a later date. THR

title: Malia Baker on Returning to ‘Descendants’ and Her Dream Roles
full_text: × Skip to main content By Naomi Jeffries Plus Icon Naomi Jeffries Intern View All July 24, 2026 4:45pm Malia Baker stars in the latest ‘Descendants’ film. Cibelle Levi As Descendants enters a new chapter, so does Malia Baker . The 19-year-old Botswana-born actress returns as Chloe Charming in Descendants: Wicked Wonderland , stepping back into the Disney franchise, not as the newcomer who once idolized the original cast, but as one of the faces leading its next generation. “It’s like entering this world as camp counselors this time instead of these nervous campers that we were the first time around,” Baker tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. Related Stories TV 'Descendants: Wicked Wonderland' Stars Malia Baker, Kylie Cantrall Talk Heroes vs. Villains, Favorite Songs and Hopes for a Sixth Film Business Disney Cutting Hundreds More Jobs in New Round of Corporate Streamlining “We put so much pressure on ourselves just because we loved the movies so much. They were so integral, not just for my formative years, but my peers as well,” she continues. “You hold so much respect and love for them, so it was a really big deal. But it was still so much fun to film.” Returning for a second film also meant welcoming a new group of cast mates, who quickly turned into some of Baker’s closest friendships. She’s excited for the “world to fall in love” with her friends and the new characters. Malia Baker. Cibelle Levi Ahead of the film’s release, the Descendants and Zombies casts embarked on a tour, giving Baker the chance to witness fan excitement firsthand. “It’s so wild to be able to literally watch it unfold in front of you and have people be so excited and joyful around something that’s so close to your heart,” she says. The Descendants films are among the most beloved Disney movies in modern time. Baker feels that the films strike a necessary chord of timeless themes and represent young people well, which is why they’ve been able to remain relevant. For Baker, stepping into the character of Chloe meant embracing the legacy of Cinderella and Prince Charming, two of Disney’s most recognizable characters. While audiences were already familiar with Chloe’s parents, the young actress had the opportunity to help define a new character entirely her own. “I think we all put our hearts and souls into it,” she says. “Yes, these are iconic characters, but Chloe Charming has never been done before, which is a lot of trust to put into a person.” Malia Baker and Brandy in ‘Descendants: Wicked Wonderland.’ Disney/David Astorga With Disney’s trust in Baker to represent the beloved character over the course of two films, she says she’s found herself growing alongside Chloe. “As things in your life start changing, you can find different levels and depths to whatever character you’re playing,” she says. “I think Chloe and I have been very fortunate to have been at very similar stages in our lives. It feels like we really are learning these lessons at the same time and inspired by one another’s growth.” The actress hopes that Wicked Wonderland viewers watch it and enjoy it. “It can seem like it’s your responsibility to not enjoy something, because it’s not as ‘serious,’” she says. “But I think there’s something really magical in being able to learn a great lesson while having fun.” While Chloe Charming may be the role she’s most known for today, sitting at the top of her acting bucket list is Starfire from Teen Titans . “I love the role of Starfire, I think she’s the coolest ever she is just such a baddie in her own right,” she says, laughing. “I would swap out the blue for some pink hair any time any place.” The actress says a role in a biopic would also be a dream for her. “I don’t know who, what or when, I keep joking with Brandy about playing her,” she says. “I told her I’ll start practicing for it.” Malia Baker. Cibelle Levi While Starfire, and maybe a Brandy biopic if she ever gives that call, remain on Baker’s manifestation board, she’s still wrapping her head around the fact that she’s become one of the faces of Disney’s newest generation with Descendants . “Sassy little me would’ve been shocked, flabbergasted, everything in between. It’s still a dream now,” Baker says of her younger self. “I have to have little reminders every now and then. I don’t think it’ll ever fully sink in, and honestly, I’m happy it won’t.” THR

title: Paramount-WBD Merger Opponents Cheer Legal Delay, Stocks Slide As Industry Absorbs Latest Plot Twist
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Dade Hayes , Jill Goldsmith July 24, 2026 4:35pm Story Arc The Paramount lot Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images After Friday’s delay in the Paramount-WBD antitrust lawsuit , shares of both media companies slid in after-hours trading, foes of the merger exulted and observers tried to process the latest twist in the merger saga. California Attorney General Rob Bonta hailed the agreement, under which Paramount pledged not close the $110 billion deal before June 1, 2027, or a legal determination of the suit’s merits, whichever comes first. The pact is “great news for audiences, movie theaters, and the many people who write, build, and create the art, news, and entertainment so many of us enjoy,” he said in a statement. “We’re eager to continue to make our case in court and celebrate another tremendous win in our effort to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day.” Related Stories News Paramount Agrees To Not Close Warner Bros. Discovery Transaction Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Are Resolved News Paramount’s Takeover Of Warner Bros. Discovery Gets EU Greenlight During a press briefing on Zoom, activists who joined the fight led by the 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America adopted a pragmatic tone. Watch on Deadline “The power of many can beat the power of money when we organize – and this is not a done deal,” said Anjuli Kronheim Katz, executive director of the Committee for the First Amendment. “We’re not also being overly presumptive that we’re going to block this merger. It’s not a full victory, but it is an important indication of the power that we’ve built and what’s possible when we organize people. There’s a lot more to do. This is going to be hard, but it is not hopeless.” Peter Murrieta, secretary-treasurer of the WGA West, joined the briefing from Comic-Con in San Diego to decry the deal’s potential to “push down our compensation for writers” or cut the output of films and series. (Paramount has described the merger as “pro-Hollywood” and disputes the assertion that it will have a negative impact on workers.) Financial Sector Reacts Paramount stock touched a 52-week low on the news before closing at $8.21 and drifting down another three cents in after-hours trading. WBD shares fell almost 1% during the trading day before sagging a bit more after the session. The financial sector was stunned by the development, which was announced with about an hour left in the trading day. Paul Nary, a management professor and M&A specialist at U. Penn’s Wharton School, posted on X that the situation will be a “more expensive adventure” given the delay. He noted the $7.2-million-per-day “ticking fee” Paramount has promised to pay WBD shareholders if the deal doesn’t close by September 30. A breakup fee of $7 billion will be owed to WBD if the deal is abandoned. Paramount “clearly saw the writing on the wall” after the judge initially granted and then extended a temporary restraining order pausing the deal, Abiel Garcia, partner at Kesselman Brantly Stockinger, told Deadline. Standards for a TRO and a preliminary injunction – the stage that would have followed the TRO – are similar, he said, noting that the judge’s TRO order contained a few key footnotes working against Paramount. They included cautions that the David Ellison-led company could not address streaming efficiency as an argument in the case; and that monies due (the ticking fee) was not a reason to accelerate the proceedings. Had the AGs been able to win a PI, “that’s a bad look” that would have further emboldened the states, said Garcia, who began his career at the California Department of Justice as a deputy attorney general. “I think they had to do this to try to keep themselves afloat and not lose control of the schedule.” The AGs have said they wanted a trial date in the winter. People familiar with the case have told Paramount will likely propose a date in November. Most experts anticipate that Paramount will appeal to the Ninth Circuit if it loses at trial, and would ultimately look to take the case to the Supreme Court. It’s not clear that the AGs would appeal. The June 1 date in Friday’s agreement appears to reflect the fact that the WBD merger agreement technically expires on June 7 if the deal hasn’t closed. The parties would need a few days to figure that out. Regardless of the exact timetable, the milestone effort to reshape Hollywood, a story that seemed to be reaching its end just two weeks ago will now have several more drama-filled chapters. Girding For Battle By skipping the preliminary injunction process, Paramount is aiming to re-orient their case as it proceeds to trial. “Paramount is saying that they have all this evidence that markets don’t work the way the AGs are saying … They’re going to try and move away from traditional markets, how things have been defined before. It’s not an easy thing to do, but it’s doable. Markets evolve and change,” Garcia said. WGA leaders noted at Friday’s presser that they’ll use the time to continue to generate support, solicit testimony and further build the case. The ticking fee and momentum from the lawsuit ‘s early traction suggest “the states will likely be in no mood to settle, at least not early on, and at least not without major concessions,” U. Penn’s Nary observed. While the frustrations of Ellison; his father, Larry Ellison, the Oracle billionaire and deal backer; and others in the Paramount camp have taken center stage in recent days, WBD also faces a difficult path. Already preparing for its fourth corporate ownership change in the past decade, employees at the company will experience confusion and inertia in the coming months. And don’t forget, for a while they believed they were being taken over by Netflix after the streaming giant sealed a deal last December, outdueling Comcast and Paramount in the initial bidding rounds. The company is “stuck in limbo for now,” Nary wrote. It “can’t make major changes to position themselves for survival if they believe the deal will fail, and can’t start the integration process/restructuring with $PSKY. From my perspective, I think this means WBD business may suffer either way, making it even more difficult for them to go back to being a reasonably well-positioned standalone firm if the deal doesn’t close, and also making Paramount’s already tough job of integrating, cost-cutting, and making this deal work if and when they do close even more of an uphill battle.” Now, a deal that was hurtling through the regulatory process at a remarkable pace, going from proposal to the verge of completion in about five months, has now entered into a period of stasis. Executives from both companies are set to report their quarterly earnings over the next couple of weeks, and will certainly encounter questions about having to revise their optimistic projections about wrapping up the deal over the summer. “The deal may still close or it may not,” Forrester Research VP Mike Proulx told the Wall Street Journal . “What we know is that the path to either outcome just got longer, messier, and likely more expensive.” ‘Spaceballs’ Cinematic Universe; ‘Rings Of Power’ News; AMC ‘Vampire’ S4 Donald Trump Delivers Rally-Like Hour Of Rehash In WHCD Speech ‘The Odyssey’s $84M+ 2nd Frame Would Be Nolan Record, Over ‘Dark Knight’ WBD Sues Amazon Saying It Poached HBO Max Marketing Exec Pia Barlow More from this Story Arc Paramount WB July 24, 2026 Paramount Agrees To Not Close Warner Bros Discovery Transaction Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Are Resolved July 23, 2026 Judge Extends Temporary Restraining Order Pausing Paramount-Warner Bros. title: Pamela Anderson Talks New Dark Comedy ‘Rosebush Pruning’, Second Chances & If ‘Baywatch’ Revisit Is In The Cards
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Rosy Cordero Rosy Cordero Associate Editor, TV @SocialRosy More Stories By Rosy Pamela Anderson Talks New Dark Comedy ‘Rosebush Pruning’, Second Chances & If ‘Baywatch’ Revisit Is In The Cards Alycia Debnam-Carey Signs With Gersh Robin Givens Joins Prime Video’s ‘Cross’ As Intellectual Conservative Senator For Season 3 View All July 24, 2026 4:26pm Pamela Anderson as Mom in 'Rosebush Pruning' Courtesy Since her critically acclaimed role in 2024’s The Last Showgirl , Pamela Anderson ‘s acting career has been moving in a new direction. With decades devoted to more mainstream roles befitting of the blonde bombshell, Anderson now embraces projects that both challenge and scare her. Up next, she stars in the satirical dark comedy Rosebush Pruning , as part of a star-studded ensemble that also includes Callum Turner, Riley Keough, Elle Fanning, Jamie Bell, Elena Anaya and Lukas Gage. The film, directed by Karim Aïnouzhits and written by Efthimis Filippou, hits select theaters across the U.S. today. Related Stories News 'Hadestown: The Musical', 'Motor City', Films By Nicolas Winding Refn, Hirokazu Koreeda, More In Indie Rush - Specialty Preview Casting 'Baywatch' Adds Blair Redford To Recurring Cast Rosebush Pruning follows a rich American family that lives in hedonistic isolation in Spain, seeking love and validation through one another, their designer wardrobes, and pop music. When an outsider infiltrates the family, buried tensions surface and blood ties are severed. Watch on Deadline While on a break from working on her garden at home, Anderson spoke to Deadline about the evolution of her career, proving herself in an industry that can often be unforgiving, and whether or not a return to Baywatch is in the stars. “I love the film Rosebush Pruning because I read the script and I knew Karim and his work, of which I was a big fan, and of the other people that are involved. It was like the hot movie. Everybody wanted to be in it, and it was just so odd and provocative. It was also great that Karim got to work with Efthimis, who normally just works with Yorgos [Lanthimos]. That was an odd and interesting pairing too,” shared Anderson. From L to R Top: Elle Fanning, Jamie Bell, Callum Turner, and Lukas Gage. Front L to R: Riley Keough and Tracy Letts. Courtesy The film will keep viewers on the edge of their seats with shocking twists and turns. Anderson plays the deceased family matriarch who lost her life after a pack of wolves savagely gobbled her up, leaving nearly nothing behind to be buried. She is, however, immortalized in concrete, as a naked woman atop a pretty empty grave outside their home. The family routinely visits the site, a tradition that’s often the cause of emotional outbursts. “There are shocking things that happen in the film to tell the story, but it’s not gratuitous. It’s just random. I think there is something to be said about this level of wealth and vapidness, the lack of empathy and awareness in this world,” the Canadian native said. Adding, “I remember when I came to Los Angeles, and people just talked about money. I thought, add zeros, add zeros. Like, someone let me think it’s $100, but they were talking about millions. I tried to find my way to navigate it all because it was way out of my depth. I’m so happy that I have had the life that I’ve had, and that I come from where I’ve come from, so I can kind of appreciate things in a different way.” Pamela Anderson in ‘The Last Showgirl’ Roadside Attractions Anderson took a quick trip down memory lane during the conversation, reflecting on how she couldn’t have imagined back then how her life would turn out. From her early credits in fan-favorite projects like Baywatch , Home Improvement , Barbwire , and two stints on Dancing With the Stars , they are fun experiences she remembers fondly. But today, she’s moving on a totally different wavelength. “I felt like I had dug a hole for myself when I was younger. It was great to be able to be in these popular TV shows and get all this attention. Then the way my personal life went and how it became tabloid fodder, I couldn’t see a serious film career for me or anyone offering me a dramatic role. But it was so nice that I got to play Roxie in Chicago on Broadway, and my son made this documentary on my life [Netflix’s Pamela, a Love Story ], and it reintroduced me to people in a different way,” Anderson stated. She added, “Then [director] Gia [Coppola] was persistent and got me to do The Last Showgirl, and I haven’t stopped since. It’s been great having indie film directors see me about really great projects. I’ve been really lucky.” Of this latest evolution, she is resolute in that she will not take anything for granted. Up next, she has a lineup of finished movies soon to be released: Place to Be from director Kornél Mundruczó, which will premiere at the Venice Film Festival; Michael Cera’s feature directorial debut Love is Not the Answer ; Somedays, starring opposite Billy Bob Thornton; the Sally Potter-directed Alma ; and playing Guy Pierce’s love interest in Rania Attieh and Daniel Garcia’s Queen of the Falls . “So now I figure, this is my second chance, or whatever you want to call it, and I’m not taking it for granted. I have nothing to lose, and I’m going to do everything to my utmost capability. I also want to see things through to the end. It’s very important when you do a movie, even if it’s a very small part, that you promote it. You have to because so many people are depending on you. I’m very proud of my work. And with this difficult time for theaters and the movie industry, we have to promote for each other, not just ourselves.” Pamela Anderson as C.J. Parker, Alexandra Paul as Lt.Stephanie Holden, Gregory Alan-Williams as Police Sgt. Garner Ellerbee, David Hasselhoff as Lt. Mitch Buchannon, David Charvet as Matt Brody, Nicole Eggert as Summer Quinn, Jeremy Jackson as Hobie Buchannon FremantleMedia With this new phase of her career going strong, there’s a lingering question about the past. Anderson’s best known for her portrayal of C.J. Parker in the 90s series Baywatch , which is currently being rebooted by Fox starring Stephen Amell, Shay Mitchell and Brooks Nader. With stars from the original series like David Chokachi and Erika Eleniak returning to Venice, would Anderson consider appearing on the new show if she were approached? “No one’s reached out to me. I don’t know much about it. I know that they were talking to my sons at some point about producing, but I don’t think they had a meeting of the minds. I’m not sure what happened there, but I wish them well. It was a great job, and I loved going to work every day on the beach. I would have been there anyway. [ Laughs ] At the time, it taught me a lot, and it gave me worldwide exposure. Everything I’ve done has led me to here, which is a blessing. But I have no plans of going back to Baywatch ,” she said. When asked if she wasn’t curious about what became of C.J., she added, “If my kids were involved, I probably would have listened to them. I think I’ve just got to keep on seeing what else is out there. I get that there’s a lot of really great TV out there right now, but I’ve already done that. Now is my time to really play with different characters. I don’t want to just fill my time until the end of the year. I have options, and some things I’m thinking about, including some theater again. I want to make really bold choices. I want to surprise people. I want to surprise myself.
