Hemecker’s credits over the years also include “Millennium,” “Ghost Whisperer,” “Numb3rs,” “The Vampire Diaries,” “Nikita,” “V,” and many more. Paramount Skydance Agrees to Link Merger Antitrust Case to Pre-Existing Paramount+ Subscriber Suit Ralph William Hemecker was born on June 12, 1961, and studied English at Bucknell University, where he was already making short films. He later took filmmaking classes at New York University. Popular on Variety Hemecker started his career in production and post-production, and early on was a director on Fox’s “America’s Most Wanted.” He also got early experience on the syndicated series “Silk Stalkings,” which he later directed episodes for, as well as Stephen J. Cannell’s “Renegade.” Another big break came in 2000, when he directed the TNT TV movie adaptation of the comic “Witchblade,” executive produced by Dan Halsted and Oliver Stone. That turned into the “Witchblade” TV series, which he served as showrunner, executive producer and writer for two seasons, from 2001 to 2002. Among his busiest gigs were directing 31 episodes of “Blue Bloods” and 28 episodes of “Once Upon a Time.” “Some losses are impossible to put into words,” “Once Upon a Time” star Lana Parilla wrote on Instagram. “ Ralph Hemecker was one of the kindest, most generous souls I’ve ever known. One of ‘Once Upon a Time’s’ defining directors. A truly passionate, beautiful man and my dear friend. I was lucky enough to shadow Ralph as a director as he knew ‘Once,’ behind the camera, best. He was always carrying a camera in hand, staying up all night in the director’s office putting his shots together, studying the scripts and endlessly visiting sets in preparation. His passion was infectious. We always knew if Ralph was directing, we were in good hands.” Wrote “Once” exec producers Adam Horowitz and Eddy Kitsis: “Ralph Hemecker was a great friend, partner, and a true artist. His contribution to ‘Once Upon a Time’ was immeasurable and he will be missed more than words can express.” Hemecker also directed feature films and television movies such as “Dead On,” “Blade Squad,” “Haunting Sarah,” “Fatal Desire,” “Nora Roberts’ Angels Fall,” “Nora Roberts’ Midnight Bayou” and “Skyrunners.” He launched Mythic Films in 2000. Hemecker is survived by two stepdaughters, as well as his father, sister, brother, three nephews, one niece and a great-nephew. Services will be announced at a later date. title: Kalshi Accuses Netflix of Defamation Over Trailer for Prediction Markets Documentary
full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All July 24, 2026 3:47pm Scott Olson/Getty Images Logo text Netflix has been threatened with legal action by Kalshi , which accuses the streaming giant of defamation over a trailer for an upcoming documentary that showed traders making wagers in a state it’s not allowed to operate. In a cease-and-desist, Kalshi demanded Netflix to immediately take down the trailer for Instadocs: The Prediction Market Games and issue a public retraction. It said that the video falsely suggests that users traded sports events contracts on Kalshi in Nevada in violation of a court order. In the trailer, a brief scene shows several people gathered at a house in Nevada discussing prediction markets during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. One participant holds up what appears to be a Kalshi transaction receipt and says, “I like betting on Kalshi” before claiming he placed a $5,000 wager on Spain to win the tournament. Related Stories Movies '72 Hours' Review: Kevin Hart Throws Himself Into the Slapstick but Netflix's Intergenerational Farce Squanders Its Premise TV Apple Gets Into the Dating Game: New Series Sends Unlikely Couples to World's Most Remote Locations The prediction market operator is currently barred from offering event-based contracts that would allow Nevada residents to place bets on sports under a court order issued as part of ongoing litigation with state regulators. The letter argued that Netflix falsely portrays the company of violating the injunction by implying that the trade in the trailer occurred in July 2026. “These false statements jeopardize Kalshi’s legal standing in litigation that is highly material to Kalshi’s business,” stated the letter, which noted that the company is concerned that the trailer could expose it to court sanctions or other penalties. Kalshi pointed to several details that it says reveal the receipt shown in the trailer isn’t authentic. Among them: The image displayed on the phone is dated May 16, 2025, more than a year before the events depicted in the trailer occurred. It also noted that the phone screen shows the word “crop,” indicating the user was viewing a saved image rather than interacting with the live Kalshi application. Leading up to the legal threat, Kalshi alerted a Netflix employee responsible for editing the trailer about the alleged inaccuracies. According to the letter, the employee acknowledged not realizing the receipt was dated from the previous year or that it appeared to be a cropped screenshot rather than a live transaction. Kalshi said the employee agreed the receipt would not appear in the finished documentary but refused to remove it from the trailer despite being warned that it could create legal complications in the Nevada litigation. Those concerns quickly materialized, with a CNN reporter subsequently contacting the company seeking clarification about where and when the featured trades occurred, Kalshi said. The company argued Netflix’s refusal to remove the trailer after learning of the alleged inaccuracies is evidence of actual malice under defamation law. In a statement, Netflix said none of the footage in the documentary was fabricated. “The footage was filmed at the Winible World Cup Watch Weekend in Las Vegas on July 17, 2026,” a spokesperson added. “The featured trader with the trade on Spain showed us a screenshot of his bet, that was made in May 2025 prior to any Nevada court order. Any specific trades or bets referenced during that weekend are between the individual and the app in which they placed the trades.” THR

title: HBO Max Leads the Emmy Drama and Comedy Races for the First Time Since 2017. How Often Do Both Frontrunners Win?
full_text: Breaking News Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial Jul 24, 2026 2:30pm PT HBO Max Leads the Emmy Drama and Comedy Races for the First Time Since 2017. How Often Do Both Frontrunners Win? Awards Circuit Column: "The Pitt" and "Hacks" look to make history for the network, along with "DTF St. Louis" on the limited side. By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest HBO Max Leads the Emmy Drama and Comedy Races for the First Time Since 2017. How Often Do Both Frontrunners Win? 13 hours ago Anne Hathaway’s Oscars ‘Odyssey’: Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? 18 hours ago Oscar Voters Rave Over Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ at First Academy Screenings: ‘The Definitive Filmmaker of Our Time’ 2 days ago See All HBO Max HBO Max wants it all. The most-nominated network enters Phase 2 of the Emmy race with the year’s two most-nominated series, giving the platform a rare opportunity to capture television’s top drama and comedy prizes, and potentially make history across three major program categories. “ The Pitt ,” the sophomore season of the breakout medical drama, leads all programs with 25 nominations. Close behind is “ Hacks ,” which earned 24 nominations, making it the most-nominated comedy series in Emmy history. The next closest is Apple TV’s horror-comedy “Widow’s Bay,” with 19. Related Stories Christopher Nolan Dedicates 'The Odyssey' to Late Imax Pioneer David Keighley Anne Hathaway's Oscars 'Odyssey': Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? It’s an uncommon achievement for a single network or platform to produce both the most-nominated drama and comedy series in the same year. Popular on Variety Apple TV accomplished the feat last year with “Severance” and “The Studio,” the latter of which became another comedy record-breaker. A year earlier, FX earned the distinction with “Shōgun” and “The Bear,” which at the time also became the most-nominated comedy series in Emmy history before ultimately losing the top comedy prize to Season 3 of “Hacks.” And now, it is HBO Max’s turn. The platform’s current dominance marks its first time leading both genres since 2017. (I misstated this distinction on this week’s episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast.) For HBO, however, this territory is familiar. The premium network led both drama and comedy nominations in consecutive years, in 2003 and 2004, with “The Sopranos,” “Six Feet Under” and “Sex and the City.” It repeated the feat during the latter half of the 2010s with “Game of Thrones,” “Westworld” and “Veep.” Few programmers in Emmy history have consistently produced the leading drama and comedy contenders in the same ceremony. History, however, shows that nomination dominance does not always translate into Emmy glory. Among the 18 instances in which a single network led the Emmy nominations in both drama and comedy, the series ultimately won only four times (22%). Those successful double victories came twice for NBC with “Hill Street Blues” and “Cheers” in 1983 and 1984, again for NBC in 1987 with “L.A. Law” and “The Golden Girls,” and, finally, for HBO in 2016 with “Game of Thrones” and “Veep.” Leading both genres reflects passion for programs for sure, but hardly guarantees a path to the big stage. Campaign strategy, momentum and voter sentiment during final-round voting will ultimately determine whether HBO Max can capitalize on its historic position and not fall to some of its closest competitors like Apple’s “Pluribus” in drama series and “Widow’s Bay” in comedy. Notably, one statistic strongly favors another win for “The Pitt.” The most-nominated program series of the Emmy year has won its corresponding top series category 41 times across 73 eligible ceremonies (56%). Last year provided a rare exception when “Severance,” with 27 nominations, lost drama series to “The Pitt.” Before that upset, the most-nominated series had won its corresponding top category every year from 2015 through 2024. “The Pitt” enters this part of the season not only with the largest nomination haul but also as the reigning champion after winning its debut season. Only four shows have won drama series for both their first and second seasons: “Hill Street Blues,” “Picket Fences,” “The West Wing” and “Mad Men.” Three of those four — except “Picket” — ultimately won at least four drama series Emmys overall. (CBS’ “Mission: Impossible” and “The Defenders” also won the top drama prize in their first two seasons when the category carried different titles: “Outstanding Dramatic Series” and “Outstanding Program Achievement in the Field of Drama,” respectively.) WIDOW’S BAY, Matthew Rhys, ‘Welcome to Widow’s Bay!’, (Season 1, ep. 101, aired April 29, 2026). photo: ©Apple TV+ / Courtesy Everett Collection ©Apple TV/Courtesy Everett Collection The stats suggest “Hacks” faces a slightly steeper climb. While the series leads the comedy field in nominations and already owns the comedy series trophy for its third season, the most-nominated comedy has historically converted at a lower rate than its drama counterpart. The most-nominated comedy series has won 25 out of 59 times in the current category format (or 42%). The frontrunner has been especially vulnerable in recent years, losing five of the past eight ceremonies, including 2023, when “The Bear” fell to “Hacks.” Also worth noting: the last comedy series to win in non-consecutive years was “Everybody Loves Raymond,” which won for its seventh season in 2003 and again for its ninth and final season in 2005, with “Arrested Development” winning in between. Other comedies to accomplish the feat include “Murphy Brown,” “Cheers,” “All in the Family” and, in the category’s earliest years, “The Jack Benny Show.” So, if HBO Max completes the coveted drama-comedy double, “The Pitt” appears to be the safer bet for a repeat victory, while “Hacks” will need to overcome some more historical statistics. The streamer also has its sights set on an even rarer accomplishment. Beef. (L to R) Oscar Isaac as Josh Martin, Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin in episode 201 of Beef. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 COURTESY OF NETFLIX In limited series, HBO Max’s “DTF St. Louis” earned 13 nominations, including directing, writing and supporting acting recognition for David Harbour, Jason Bateman, Richard Jenkins, Linda Cardellini and Joy Sunday. The network hopes to overtake Netflix’s “Beef,” which leads the limited series field with 16 nominations. The first iteration won this category. “Beef” stars Oscar Isaac and Carey Mulligan appear well-positioned in the lead acting categories, while Harbour and Cardellini face a more crowded supporting field because of their co-stars nominated from the same series. Meanwhile, Charles Melton and Yuh-jung Youn enter their respective races without internal competition. That could be helpful down the road. But here are some more numbers to consider. The limited series frontrunner has been the least reliable of the three major program categories. The most-nominated limited series has won 16 of 45 times (or 36%) — compared with 45% for drama and 42% for comedy. Since 2021, the nomination leader for miniseries has lost four out of five times: “WandaVision” (2021), “Dahmer – Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story” (2023), “True Detective: Night Country” (2024) and “The Penguin” (2025), which led with 23 nominations but lost to “Adolescence.” Only “The White Lotus” (2022) managed a victory. The category has long produced “frontrunner” collapses, including HBO’s “Mildred Pierce” (20 nominations, 2011), which lost to “Downton Abbey,” and CBS’ “Lonesome Dove” (15 nominations, 1989), which fell to “War and Remembrance.” Winning the top series prizes in drama, comedy and limited series in the same year remains one of the rarest accomplishments in Emmy history. It has happened only three times: HBO achieved the feat in 2015 with “Game of Thrones,” “Veep” and “Olive Kitteridge,” while NBC accomplished it twice, in 1996 with “ER,” “Frasier” and “Gulliver’s Travels,” and in 1987 with “L.A. Law,” “The Golden Girls” and “A Year in the Life.” So in fairness, HBO has done it before. But can they do it again? That remains to be determined. But it is still early in Phase 2, and plenty can change before ballots are finalized. Final-round voting runs Aug. 17-26 ahead of the Creative Arts Emmy Awards and Governors Gala on Sept. 5-6. The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards will air Sept. 14 on NBC. The show stars Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan, a veteran Green Lantern, and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, Jordan’s protege who is learning the ropes. The heroes have magical rings that allow them to create any object imaginable out of green light. They patrol the galaxy and keep peace as members of the Green Lantern Corps. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial The cast includes Kelly Macdonald, Laura Linney, Paula Patton, Garret Dillahunt, Poorna Jagannathan, Nicole Ari Parker, Jason Ritter, Sherman Augustus, Paul Ben-Victor and Ulrich Thomsen as the classic Green Lantern villain Sinestro. title: Noah Wyle on ‘The Pitt’ Fan Discourse, Saving Hollywood and What’s Coming In Season 3
full_text: Breaking News Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial Jul 24, 2026 1:30pm PT Noah Wyle on ‘The Pitt’ Fan Discourse, Saving Hollywood and What’s Coming In Season 3 Awards Circuit Podcast: Also on this episode, the Roundtable dives into the TV Academy's controversial move of five categories out of the Emmy telecast By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest ‘Blue Bloods,’ ‘Once Upon a Time’ TV Director Ralph W. Hemecker Dies at 65 11 hours ago ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ Co-Creator Bill Prady Explains the Science Behind the Show’s Multiverse 1 day ago Shaking Up the Emmys By Moving Five Categories Out of the Telecast Might Not Work, But at Least the TV Academy Is Trying Something 1 day ago See All Chantal Anderson for Variety Noah Wyle knows some “ The Pitt ” fans came down hard on his character, Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, given how the character’s personal struggles caused him to lash out at some of his colleagues in Season 2. But he tries not to pay attention to the online discourse. “The blending of the line between actor and part that I sometimes see, where an actor is blamed for the behavior of a character, or where a character’s dialog stops being representative of the character and starts being representative of the creative team — as if they’re saying something that they believe through this particular vehicle — I think gotten a little blurry as viewers have sort of conflated character message and character,” he tells Variety ‘s Awards Circuit Podcast . “It doesn’t necessarily have an encoded message because somebody’s saying it. Other than the dramatic tension within that one scene, it’s not necessarily trying to be representative of anything larger.” Related Stories Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial States Sue to Block Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Defying DOJ Wyle says he believes it’s still just a small but very vocal portion of the viewership that is piling on — but he prefers not to be engaged with the more negative conversations that might be out there. “My skin is is too thin to really engage anything that might be coming at me, so I tend to want to say live and let live, and I’ll go do my job, and you can take what you want from me.” Popular on Variety Wyle does say that his son would sometimes warn him when the backlash against Dr. Robby got very heated online: “My son is the one who calls me and goes, ‘Dad, they’re really mad at you.’ He’s my firewall. He’ll go, ‘Dad, you might not want to go to the market today unless you start treating Dr. Mohan better!” Wyle understands that the vitriol that came at Dr. Robby this year “was disappointment that he was acting less heroic than he presented himself last year. But when we’re at our most desperate, we’re not always our most graceful. And we were trying to show somebody who was going through a mental health crisis and was behaving irresponsibly, unprofessionally and out of character for himself as he was asking people to see him in his moment of plight and potentially stop him from doing himself harm. That did get misinterpreted by some people as him just being misogynistic or cruel. I think there was a much bigger picture at play.” On this edition of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, “The Pitt” star, executive producer and director Noah Wyle — Emmy-nominated three times this year — discusses the wild fan reaction to Season 2 and Dr. Robby’s storyline, as well as how “The Pitt” is showing how to keep production jobs in Los Angeles. But first, the Roundtable looks at the TV Academy’s decision to move five categories out of the Emmy telecast and the debate over whether this will make a difference in producing a more entertaining ceremony. Listen below! Wyle has been a big advocate of bringing production back to Los Angeles, and “The Pitt” — shot locally here on the Warner Bros. lot — has put him front and center in the conversation. “I’m looking at it from the standpoint of somebody who has grown up in and around this industry and befriended people who are generations deep in this industry who’ve watched it really crater over the last couple years,” he says. “There is still an abundance of talent here, and ‘The Pitt’ is is proof of what you could do with that talent when you when you apply it. That, I feel, is being grossly overlooked in the pursuit of tax credits or to circumvent union protections, as work not only leaves the state but leaves the country. “I think ‘The Pitt’ economically has proven that it’s still cost-effective to shoot in Los Angeles if you keep your footprint small and you make certain considerations at the outset that in the event of a success, a rising tide lifts all boats,” he adds. “When we started shooting the pit on the Warner Bros. lot, it was a bit of a ghost town. The only thing that was happening there were the tours going through empty sound stages, talking about the work that used to be done there. And now it’s a fairly buzzy place, so I’m hoping that there’s a trend.” Despite some of the rougher discourse we mentioned above, Wyle says he’s pleased that most of the reaction about Dr. Robby’s mental health journey in Season 2 has been positive. “We hoped that once you got past the architecture of the protagonist having a nervous breakdown in a mass casualty event, the aggregate toll of an average shift in the average life of an average career would be compelling enough television,” he says. “And Season 2 was a bit more speculative than one because of that, and more gratifying to see the response, because it reaffirms that there’s a narrative here that doesn’t necessarily need to revolve around a stunt, like an air show disaster or something massive to really keep viewers’ attention. “It’s incredibly gratifying to be on a show that has resonance and is being spoken about at all,” he adds. “It’s also really gratifying to be involved in a show that’s saying something that sparks conversation and of an intimate nature. You want to be a water cooler show. You want things that people have differing opinions on, so that those ideas and debates can happen in the marketplace, and people can arrive at consensus and hopefully find commonality in that process. I think a lot more bridges have been built through this show than have been burned.” As for next season, the show is moving to November — a chilly month that will provide a bit of contrast to what we’ve seen so far. “We wanted to play with a different season,” Wyle says. “We just came off of hot July 4, so it seemed appropriate to plot it a little into a different season. We wanted Robby to have been away from the hospital for a little while, and so both of those things felt like fall would be appropriate. Everybody’s turning on their heaters again. The first rains caused slick roadways, different kind of cases, different asthetic.” Wyle’s first appearance in Variety was on Feb. 9, 1990, for the NBC miniseries “Blind Faith.” “Given my level of participation in that event, my grandfather watched both segments and said, ‘I had to watch an awful lot of Blind Faith for a little bit of Noah,'” Wyle recalls. “The real story is that somebody had told me that you had to say seven words to get a SAG card, and my line was five words long. It was ‘What’s going on down there?!’ I spent all morning trying to figure out how to stretch it to seven. And when the director said action, I said ‘Excuse me, what’s going on down there?!’ And then I found out it didn’t matter. I didn’t have to say seven words.” 10 QUESTIONS WITH NOAH WYLE: 1. Childhood nickname: “‘Wile E Coyote,’ from ‘Road Runner,’ I got called Wile E. Coyote a lot growing up, or ‘Noah’s Ark,’ obviously.” 2. Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into it now: “Oh my goodness, I’m still into everything I was into as a kid. But I had an unnatural obsession with ‘Grease 2.’ I know every word to ‘Grease 2,’ and sometimes alone in my car, will do renditions of ‘Cool Rider.’ I’ve befriended Chris McDonald, who played Goose, he was the tall T-Bird, and I’m sure he’s so annoyed with how many times I bring that movie up.” 3. Go-to Karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song: “It’s a massive phobia that I’ve been grappling with for most of my life. I got shamed young and scared to sing publicly, so it’s been one of my great desires to be able to have confidence. Even the mention of the word ‘karaoke’ makes me break out and sweat. Because it usually means I’m being forced to do something I’m not comfortable with. But I’m working on it. I usually warm up slow with something that Rex Harrison could handle.” [What about alone in the shower?] “That’s when I go full ‘Dreamgirls’ cast album.” 4. Give me an alternate title for your show: [Not asked] 5. What’s your secret talent? : “Acting. Don’t tell anybody. It’s my only talent.” 6. Favorite ice cream flavor : “I like McConnell’s mint chip ice cream a lot, but I also like peanut butter and chocolate ice cream from Haagen Dazs. That was when I got in my youth a lot. And I was part of the ’70s sherbert craze.” 7. The one item you couldn’t live without : “My wife. I’m not calling my wife an item. I’m just saying that I really, really depend heavily upon her.” 8. What TV show in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of? : “‘Deadwood,’ without hesitation. I’ve always wanted to do a western, and I loved that show. David Milch’s writing was poetry punctuated with profanity, and I would have given anything to have been in the room with Ian McShane and Tim Olyphant and Keith Carradine and some of the actors on that show. I just loved it. We had Brad Dourif, who played the doctor on ‘Deadwood.’ He’s the father of Fiona Dourif, who plays Dr. McKay. I got to tell him how much I enjoyed his performance, which I thought was so flawless. That man could put more intention into a syllable than anybody I know.” 9. Fictional character you most admire : “I most admire Atticus Finch, probably. It’s infused with Gregory Peck’s performance. I saw it at a formative age, and there’s that moment at the end when up at the balcony, Jim and Scout are told to stand. ‘Stand up, Jim, your father’s passing.’ And the quiet dignity and heroism of Atticus always loomed large for me.” 10. Your favorite piece of advice : “The first one that comes to mind is George Clooney early on saying, ‘Take your work seriously. Don’t take yourself seriously.’ That was a big one. I remember I saw an interview once with former Boston Celtic great Bill Russell — and I don’t like giving any credit to anything Boston Celtic, but Bill Russell is not your average Boston Celtic — and he said that he learned later in life that it was far better to understand than it is to be understood. And that we spend so much time trying to get our own personal points of view across, and so little time trying to listen to everybody else’s, that we sometimes do ourselves a disservice. So I latched onto that one too.” Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. title: Euro Cinema Body UNIC Says EU Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Deal Approval Conditions "Should…
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Oscar Documentary Contender ‘House Of Hope’ Secures North American Distribution Film Financiers & Producers Flock To Inaugural African Film Investor Roundtable In Cape Town Venice Head Talks Studio Absence, Dearth Of Female Golden Lion Contenders & Why Neon Nixed Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ – Q&A View All July 23, 2026 9:35am Story Arc Getty Images The Brussels-based International Union of Cinemas (UNIC), representing exhibitors in 39 European territories, has said the European Commission’s conditions for its recent approval of Paramount ’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery should have gone further. Related Stories News Paramount’s Takeover Of Warner Bros. Discovery Gets EU Greenlight News Analysis: As The New UK Prime Minister Cosies Up To Donald Trump, Lisa Nandy Could Be About To Become The Most Consequential Culture Secretary In America In Recent Memory The body was reacting to the EC’s announcement Wednesday that it had approved Paramount Skydance’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) on the condition that divests its stake in United International Pictures (UIP), the film distribution venture it currently jointly owns with Universal Pictures. “UNIC welcomes the Commission’s decision to require the divestment of Paramount’s stake in UIP and additional requirements. While it addresses an important competition concern, we strongly believe that the Commission could and should have gone further with its conditions for the merger’s approval,” said UNIC CEO Laura Houlgatte. “Our sector raised numerous concerns with its competition department about the proposed deal, and the Commission’s findings don’t reflect that bigger picture. It has based its decision on too narrow a scope.” Watch on Deadline Beyond the divestment of its UIP stake, the EC ruling also stipulated that for a period of ten years, Paramount cannot directly or indirectly enter into any agreement or understanding with Universal to jointly co-distribute films in the European Economic Area (EEA), or shift the distribution of Warner films from Warner’s existing distributor to the theatrical distributor used by Paramount, where that distributor also distributes Universal’s or Disney’s films in all UIP countries in the EEA. Additionally, in the UIP countries in the EEA where Paramount and Universal do not share the same distributor, it will not be allowed to shift the distribution of Paramount’s films from Paramount’s existing distributor to the theatrical distributor used by Warner, where that distributor also distributes Universal’s or Disney’s films. The countries covered by the conditions span Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, Cyprus, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden. UNIC said the stipulations should have gone beyond the EEA territories where UIP currently operates, while the ruling also failed to address other issues such as theatrical windows and access to back catalogues. “We regret that the decision does not address similar risks arising from theatrical distribution arrangements outside the UIP territories, nor does it extend to remedies addressing theatrical windows, film diversity, preservation of film output and production pipelines, contractual practices and access to back catalogues,” said Houlgatte. “Given that the transaction continues to face legal challenges based on such factors in the United States, it is clear that these broader concerns about the merger remain unresolved and unanswered. UNIC will keep a close eye on developments in the US and any potential consequences for Europe .” Houlgatte added that UNIC was also disappointed that the European Media Board, an independent advisory body, had not examined the wider implications of the transaction for media pluralism, cultural diversity and the audiovisual market. ‘Spaceballs’ Cinematic Universe; ‘Rings Of Power’ News; AMC ‘Vampire’ S4 Donald Trump Delivers Rally-Like Hour Of Rehash In WHCD Speech ‘The Odyssey’s $84M+ 2nd Frame Would Be Nolan Record, Over ‘Dark Knight’ WBD Sues Amazon Saying It Poached HBO Max Marketing Exec Pia Barlow More from this Story Arc Paramount WB July 24, 2026 Paramount-WBD Merger Opponents Cheer Legal Delay, Stocks Slide As Industry Absorbs Latest Plot Twist July 24, 2026 Paramount Agrees To Not Close Warner Bros Discovery Transaction Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Are Resolved View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: Paramount Seeks Three-Day Evidentiary Hearing As Judge Considers Preliminary Injunction To Halt…
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Resolved; Opponents Cheer Delay; Stocks Slide Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Paramount Agrees To Not Close Warner Bros Discovery Transaction Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Are Resolved Former ‘60 Minutes’ Correspondent Cecilia Vega Details Claims CBS News Brass Wanted Her To Insert Political Bias In Stories What To Expect As Donald Trump Attends The Rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner; Watch The Livestream View All July 23, 2026 12:21pm Story Arc Getty Images UPDATED, with state AG and WGA response: Paramount is proposing that a federal judge hold a three-day evidentiary hearing later in August as she weighs whether to issue a preliminary injunction that would halt its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery as legal proceedings play out. Related Stories News Paramount’s Takeover Of Warner Bros. Discovery Gets EU Greenlight Legal Writers Guild Seeks Preliminary Injunction To Halt Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery Merger; Wants Case Timing Aligned With State AG Suit U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a temporary restraining order on Monday, halting the transaction for two weeks, while she set a hearing for Aug. 3 on a lengthier preliminary injunction. The order was issued in response to an antitrust lawsuit brought by California and 11 other states last week. In a filing on Wednesday, Paramount’s legal team is seeking essentially a mini-trial, to be held the week of August 17 or August 24. They also said that the company would consent to an extension of the TRO “to cover the period through a decision by the Court.” Watch on Deadline Paramount’s lawyers wrote that the state AGs are seeking an “extraordinary and drastic remedy” — a preliminary injunction that would pause the merger for at least eight months — without giving the company “an opportunity for a full and fair hearing.” They wrote that the judge “has already recognized Defendants’ proof ‘creates disputes regarding the facts’ that need to be resolved to fully analyze the competitive effects of the transaction. … An evidentiary hearing would allow the Court to do so regarding critical factual issues including market definition, real-world competitive dynamics, barriers to expansion, and incentives. Resolving these factual disputes is essential to answering the fundamental question of whether Plaintiffs have carried their burden to prove that the proposed transaction substantially lessens competition. It does not.” Hanging over all of this is the date of Sept. 30, after which Paramount will owe a $7 million per day “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery if the deal is not closed by then. Paramount’s legal team, led by Jeffrey Kessler, noted that in their latest brief, writing that a preliminary injunction would create “commercial uncertainty regarding the transaction and cost Paramount well over $1 billion in ticking fees and other additional costs.” The judge set a briefing schedule in which the state AGs opening brief due on Thursday, and the company response is due on Monday. The state AG reply is due on July 30. Paramount’s legal team proposed a schedule in which opening briefs would be filed on July 28, the company reply on August 7 and the AG response on August 12. The state AGs indicated their opposition to the change in schedule, arguing that Paramount now seeks to “upend” it “at the eleventh hour.” At the hearing on a TRO last week, the attorney for the state AGs, James Weingarten, opposed an earlier Paramount scheduling proposal, which he said was intended to speed up the proceedings. “Having two experts in a food fight in a month will just waste everyone’s time and resources, if it’s even possible,” he said. The Writers Guild of America filed its own motion for a preliminary injunction as part of is separate lawsuit, and is seeking to align its hearing with the states on August 3. Paramount’s legal team wrote that such a schedule was “not feasible,” but that it would be possible for a later date in August. In a filing on Thursday, the WGA legal team objected to Paramount’s proposed schedule. They wrote, “Defendants suggest that the Court cannot fairly resolve the PI Motion without a fuller evidentiary record. Not so. No party has taken any discovery in this case. Defendants have not produced a single document or piece of data to Plaintiffs; and Plaintiffs have not deposed a single Defendant witness. Without discovery to support vigorous cross-examination, Plaintiffs would be faced with Defendants’ executives’ self-serving testimony.” ‘Spaceballs’ Cinematic Universe; ‘Rings Of Power’ News; AMC ‘Vampire’ S4 Donald Trump Delivers Rally-Like Hour Of Rehash In WHCD Speech ‘The Odyssey’s $84M+ 2nd Frame Would Be Nolan Record, Over ‘Dark Knight’ WBD Sues Amazon Saying It Poached HBO Max Marketing Exec Pia Barlow More from this Story Arc Paramount WB July 24, 2026 Paramount-WBD Merger Opponents Cheer Legal Delay, Stocks Slide As Industry Absorbs Latest Plot Twist July 24, 2026 Paramount Agrees To Not Close Warner Bros Discovery Transaction Until Next Year Or Until Lawsuit Merits Are Resolved View All Story Arc Read More About: 5 Comments
